Picking up Kim's "auditing of definitions" item (and @Rémy Degenne overlay idea) — we've been building something squarely in this direction and it's deliberately project-agnostic, so Tau Ceti could be a consumer rather than the owner.

The repo is math-commons/formalization-assurance. The premise is exactly the gap Kim names: the kernel certifies proofs, not that a definition means what its name claims, that a theorem is non-vacuous, or that an axiom is true. So it specifies artifacts a mathematician can audit without reading the proofs:

  • Object-contract cards — one per constructed object: an informal description + textbook source, the Lean signature only, a characterization stated as id'd claims including at least one anti-degeneracy clause (what would make it the wrong / hack object), and a known_values test matrix (instance → expected → theorem → status). Differential testing for definitions.
  • Status is kernel-derived, so it can't be fudged — each cell's status comes from #print axioms (PROVEN_CORE_AXIOMS / proven_via_axiom / proven_mod_axioms / sorry), plus a closure-status axis (discharged / declared-on-closure / declared-off-closure) so "every headline is axiom-clean" and "N axioms still declared" never get conflated.
  • Two prose companions — FAITHFULNESS.md (the informal↔formal dictionary) and VALIDATION.md (acceptance/characterization, up to a categorical "the spec has exactly one model" certificate).
  • Axioms are vetted, not just assumed — where a development rests on an axiom, it carries a captured soundness review (is it true, non-vacuous, of the right strength?) — cross-model deep-think + literature + self-audit, with a rating and an L0–L3 strictness ladder, as a durable per-axiom record. That's the "is the axiom true?" gap above; #print axioms + the closure-status axis then track where each vetted axiom sits.

A worked example: the graphons library adopts the conventions end-to-end — a suite of known_values object-contract cards (homDensity, Graphon, cutNorm, cutDist, GraphonSpace; rows backed by #print axioms pins, each with an explicit anti-degeneracy clause), per-axiom vetting records, a closure-status axiom audit, and the reusable CI assurance gate. The hille-yosida project we are submitting to Tau Ceti is another (simpler) example.

This feels close to the "overlay for human auditing of chains of definitions" Rémy described. @Rémy Degenne — does this line up with what you had in mind, and what's missing for a shared, project-agnostic version?

My WIP attempt at producing help for auditing definitions is explained at #Lean Machine Learning > Auto-generated exposition.
The code at https://github.com/LeanMachineLearning/exposition/ is used in CI for the repository https://github.com/LeanMachineLearning/LML to produce the webpages at https://leanmachinelearning.org/LML/exposition/ . The website generation tool could be run on an other repository and is not tied to the LML library (although the pages use css that fits that library website). I am also testing it on my Brownian motion project at https://github.com/RemyDegenne/brownian-motion.

Some characteristics:

  • my main focus was on the "details" pages for each declaration, like https://leanmachinelearning.org/LML/exposition/chapter-online/module-online-bandit-algorithms-etc/decl-Bandits___ETC___regret_le/ . That page shows a theorem, then its dependency graph, then cards for all its dependencies.
  • the goal is to give a succinct view of all dependencies of a declaration, so that it's easier to make sense of it: you have on one page all the definitions of the project you need to understand to make sure the theorem says what it claims. It assumes you trust other projects you depend on, and does not list those.
  • the graph views are unreadable placeholders. They should be replaced. Kim gave helpful suggestions on the LML topic.
  • apart from the docstring texts, everything is generated from the Lean code: the dependencies are not manually annotated like in a blueprint tool, but inferred.
  • at the top of the details page, there is a link "Minimal Lean file" which opens an editor with code for the minimal dependencies up to the main declaration of the page, in the style of a comparator challenge. (I did not test their use with comparator yet). Those have two purposes: first they could eventually be used with comparator to check important results, and second they test the code that generates the dependency lists (and getting the Lean files to compile uncovered many bugs!)
  • I am designing for a library that does not accept new axioms nor sorry, so I'm not developing anything specific for those. Also, there a priori is no single "formalization target": I'm generating details pages and Lean challenge files for every single declaration (that is not an automatically generated auxiliary declaration).
  • It's WIP and still rough. Several features could probably be added, but I want to keep a clear distinction between what is generated from Lean and what is human input. We should not present human validation and machine-generated audits on the same level.

@Michael R Douglas I like some of the ideas in your formalization-assurance repo. But I am also noticing a lot of internal friction coming from the fact that all of this is heavily LLM-influence, if not completely LLM-generated:

  • I would strongly prefer if the rules and guidelines for validating (and trusting) AI-generated maths were laid down by humans and not by LLMs
  • There's a lot of lingo that wants to inspire confidence but is using obscure/new jargon at the same time

That’s reasonable, the ideas are human generated but the writing is mostly LLM and could be greatly improved. In response to the comments above on axioms and sorrys, let me add that the framework is modular and a given project will only use part of it, so projects without sorry/axiom can just leave out those files.
I don't want to sound naif, but if most of the writing is done by an LLM, who is supposed to read it? It might be terribly boring...
I did more work on the repository auditing tools that I mentioned above. See #AI authored projects > Referee

So after talking to @Kevin Buzzard and @Johan Commelin I was looking at this referee and I think its really neat, I particularly like the graph of what you need to understand to understand a given defn/result.

There are a few things I would like it to do which I don't know if it supports (but maybe its just me being wrong). But I made this which sort of captures what I would like to see. Specifically, it would be good to be able for both humans and AIs to leave a review on a particular defn or theorem. We could also include a list of "unit tests" that each defn or theorem has passed. All of this to essentially give a rating to the particular defn/theorem, i.e. the more reviews and more tests then the more likely it is to be correct and trustworthy.

For Tau Ceti I also made a list of named defns/theorems (coming from the roadmaps) which are likely to be the things we humans actually care about reviewing/checking is correct (compared to any random lemma or defn a LLM made).

Note this would also add a line to the doc string saying how many reviews and tests a particular dec has and a link to the page showing them. The idea being you could see this from the code when you hover over a defn or theorem.

@Christian Merten has built something close to my Referee that incorporates reviews from several people, like you suggest. I also updated Referee quite a bit and it now has features to better highlight interesting theorems (for example those in a formalization.yaml or a comparator config, but that does not apply to TauCeti). I also coded an attribute to indicate which theorems about a definition are important properties, which Referee then reports on the page. With Christian we talked about our respective projects and decided to build something together.
Let's find some time to talk about what you would like to see in such a tool. I'll DM you.
That sounds great. I only made that as an example of functionality I'd like to see, so if this could all feed into a single tool that would definitely be the way to go!

My thoughts on this general topic are still actively developing, but here is a bit of a braindump:

  • We really need tools like this. And we'll only need them more and more in the future.
  • It's probably good that several people are exploring this space and building various different tools to experiment.
  • But there's a risk of fragmentation, especially if the tools can not communicate with each other.
  • If we can quickly converge on some sort of protocol for sharing "reviews" or "trusted definitions" or something like that, then we can have a wider range of tools that are aimed at "wide audience", "power user", "visualisation", "performing review / adding new trust", "exploring what's trusted", etc... We wouldn't need one tool to cover all the features that one might think of.

I agree that we should build a suite of tools, not one that tries to catch everything, especially for the front end. In my current view, the types of tools we want are the following:

  1. tools to surface or inject data about the code. Examples: the characterization attribute I wrote to state that some def is the unique object with some properties up to a relation, or weaker versions that just state that some lemma is an important property of a definition; attributes that could declare what the "true" domain of a total function is; attributes like the stacks tags that link to informal corpora, etc.
  2. tools to gather data from the code and from the first tool type: computation of the minimal graph of the construction of a def (and verification that it's right); computation of an alternative graph based on a characterization if there is one; detection of the use of a value of a function outside of its intended domain...
  3. visualization and interactive tools: review view for a Lean expert, exploration view for a non-expert user, etc. Those can be particularly diverse and relatively cheap to make once we have all the data-generating and gathering tools
  4. Storage, sharing and treatment of data that comes for the interaction with (3), like reviews. Or like challenges: a user of a review tool (human or AI) could raise a challenge and ask the library contributors to prove that their definition has a property you expect (edit: I see that Chris' demo has that feature!).

Those are all good suggestions! Thanks.

Do you also have ideas about what the underlying protocol/data-format might look like? On which such tools operate...

Suggestions for the protocol:

  • "trust certificates" are a semantic hash and an informal description together with metadata (metadata can be: commit in a github repo, author)
  • certificates are signed with a PGP key by the "trusting party"
  • "trust servers" are databases that hold certificates with a federation protocol to exchange and distribute certificates between servers

This is more or less what https://github.com/chrisflav/trust-server implements.

Starting from @Christian Merten 's trust tools, my Referee website, the website @Chris Birkbeck made above and the semantic_hash repository of @Adam Topaz, I've made a attempt at a suite of tools and specifications. It's a work in progress (in particular the specifications should be discussed) and I expect that Christian and I will change several aspects of the tools.

Demo page here (AI-written overview page with links): https://leantrustbuilders.github.io/mathlib-probability-evidence/.
The demo contains several websites that copy the ones made by Christian, Chris and myself, but they all use the specifications and tools of the other repositories. In particular, they can all share their reviews.
That page also has a graph that explains how the data flows through the tools.

The repositories contain many independent things: some tools to add information to a Lean library, an extractor that builds a dataset from the library, evidence stores for reviews about the declarations, a tool that takes dataset and evidence together to derive more facts, and finally several websites that present the info to a user and send the user's inputs back to evidence stores.
Main repositories:

  • specs: specifications. S1: how to refer to a declaration; S2: what a dataset generated from a library contains; S3: how to describe external evidence (reviews, etc.) about a library.
  • annotations: new attributes that one can put on definitions to declare their intended domain, or the fact that something characterizes a definition
  • meaning-graph: computation of a "meaning" graph for a statement, and hashes that depend only on the ancestors in that graph. Similar to semantic_hash, but not importing it because we want the hashes and the graph to fit each other (one should change iff the other does), and our graph prunes more things than the one implied by semantic_hash would. The hashes are also part of the S1 spec of how to iudentify a definition, so they are a central part of the whole system.
  • extractor: the tools that build an S2 dataset from a library and the tools above. And tests about those. In particular, we can test that the meaning graph is sufficient and does not prune too much (verified on all of Mathlib, can be a CI step).
  • evidence-store: a store for evidence (reviews, comments, challenges...) as a github repository. An evidence store can import the content of an other store: particularly useful if several repositories import the same upstream repo and want to share their reviews.
  • evidence-core: takes a dataset and evidence, and computes derived things like the fact that a review is stale because the definition changed since then (detected by a hash change).
  • several user interfaces to view the data and input reviews or challenges. They are copies of the various websites people made before and my goal there was to show how all those could use the specs and tools.

Oh this is great, so let me see if I understand it, there is a common system that you can then view it in in referee, trust, tau ceti, etc. Is the idea to then combine these different views into some common version? or some system where you pick what bits you want to display for each separate project?

I really like the graphs in referee and trust. What I think would be neat is to be able to click on a node, see the declaration and the AI and humans that have trusted it, the tests, etc that are in the demo I made. But I guess if I wanted I could just build that on top of this LeanTrustBuilder framework.

I did not work at all on a new front-end that would combine the good ideas of the existing ones. I focused on getting the tools behind it working. As you write, that's a common system for storing and generating data, that you can then view with in all the websites (by modifying them slightly so that they take the data in its standardized form). I modified Referee a bit to show the reviews (but not for the things you click in the graph, apparently -- I did not check carefully): https://leantrustbuilders.github.io/mathlib-probability-evidence/site/#/d/ProbabilityTheory.strong_law_ae

The main idea is that all the features of the websites in the demo are easy to generate given the data-handling tools behind, and you should be able to tell an AI to make a new website with any combination of those features and get something working quite easily.
I think that the way to go, the framework is whats most important here.

And you could make several websites for different people (experts in Lean or not, etc.), and the reviews, challenges, questions generated by those people on the websites all are in the same format and can be aggregated (and shown back in all the views, if the view chooses to).
